Knowledge and understanding. Students have knowledge and understanding of:
1.    the concepts and terminology within the field of language learning and socialization in diverse contexts
 2.    the most important research methods and research techniques within the field of language learning and socialization
 3.    important themes within the field of language learning and socialization, such as bilingualism and multilingualism, second language learning, the role of input and interaction, home language and school language, the multicultural classroom, intercultural education, educational policy and school success of minority groups. 

Skills. Students can apply the scientific methods and techniques as used in research in the field of language learning and socialization and communicate in an academic way. They can:
4.    find relevant literature, read it critically, process and discuss it
 5.    collect, analyze, compare and contrast data
 6.    formulate research questions and answer these questions by conducting a practical or theoretical study
 7.    write a research paper in an academic manner.

Character. Students can:
8.    judge and evaluate on formal grounds and in terms of content their own research and other products and those of fellow scholars
 9.    share knowledge and contribute to discussions in a group, to put forward relevant points of view and to understand and appreciate points of views of other

How do children become members of a cultural community? In order to be an active and competent member, they not only have to learn the language, but also the (implicit) cultural norms, rules and routines of this community. In other words, they have to acquire both linguistic and cultural competence.
This is the case for children growing up and learning the language(s) and culture(s) of their parents (primary socialization process), but also when they are entering and becoming part of a new community. Nowadays, most people are part of different communities; they are multilingual and multicultural. They have to learn the linguistic and cultural competencies needed for participating in each of their communities. When entering a new community, children must learn to understand and use linguistic structures in appropriate ways. Besides, they have to learn ways to participate adequately in the sociocultural practices of the community.

In this course, we focus on the socialization process of children into the linguistic and sociocultural practices of a community. The socialization process, by which they become multilingual and multicultural, takes place in intercultural contact with members of the community, both in formal life organized in institutions as in informal daily life and in online communication.

The focus of attention in this course will be on processes of language learning and socialization. The processes will be studied from an individual and a societal perspective, in both formal and informal settings (home, online, school). The course consists of two main parts:

Part I. The individual perspective
In this part, the focus is on first language learning and bilingualism in the preschool years at home. We will deal with language learning theories by reflecting on the essence of human language, the role of age in language learning, the role of input and interaction and the learning of sounds, words, grammar and pragmatics. Next to this, we will go into bilingual development and second language learning. Attention will also be given to online language learning and socialization by exploring in what ways young children engage with popular culture, media and digital texts in their earliest years.   

Part II. The societal perspective
In this part, we focus on the formal learning environment of (pre-)school and the ways in which children are introduced in the linguistic and cultural norms of these contexts. The focus is on the institutional practices regarding language learning and multilingualism in schools. Dealing with multilingualism in the classroom, school success, and the place of language/s in the curriculum are explored. Underachievement and its social and linguistic causes among language minority students are examined. Issues such as multilingualism and educational policy, intercultural education, and minority language teaching are examined. National and international perspectives are presented.

Specifics:
The end grade of the course is based on:

  • Written exam: 60%
  • Research paper (group assignment): 40%

Students need to obtain a sufficient grade for the written exam in order to successfully complete the course.


Academic writing is part of the written assignment, which can be written in English or in Dutch. Students will provide peer feedback on the assignments, focusing on academic writing. Next to that, teacher feedback will help students develop an academic writing style.
